title: Achaemenid Empire
subtitle: 550–330 BC · Cyrus's Conquests to the Fall of Darius III

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Achaemenid kings — from Cyrus's conquests to Darius III's fall

entries.label: Cyrus II (the Great) — founder of the empire
entries.hint: Cyrus united the Persians and Medes, overthrew his grandfather Astyages of Media (c.550 BC), conquered Lydia under Croesus (c.547 BC), and took Babylon without a siege in 539 BC. He died in 530 BC campaigning against the Massagetae on the empire's eastern steppe frontier.
entries.note: Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum ME 90920); Nabonidus Chronicle (BM 35382); Herodotus, Histories 1.46–214.

entries.label: Cambyses II — the conquest of Egypt
entries.hint: Cambyses defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium in 525 BC and was crowned Pharaoh at Memphis, founding Egypt's Twenty-Seventh (Persian) Dynasty. He died in 522 BC on the road home from Egypt, as news reached him of a usurpation at the heart of the empire.
entries.note: Udjahorresnet inscription (Vatican Museums, Naophorous statue); Behistun Inscription (DB) §11; Herodotus, Histories 3.1–38.

entries.group: Darius I and the Imperial System
entries.label: Bardiya (Gaumata) — the pretender king
entries.hint: For roughly seven months a man Darius's own inscription names as the magus Gaumata ruled as Bardiya, claiming to be Cyrus's surviving son. Darius's account — the only detailed source — calls him an impostor and the dead prince's murderer; modern historians note this is exactly the story a usurper would need to tell, and the truth beneath it cannot be fully recovered.
entries.note: Behistun Inscription (DB) §§10–13; Herodotus, Histories 3.61–79.

entries.group: Darius I and the Imperial System
entries.label: Darius I — the imperial system
entries.hint: Darius killed Gaumata with six noble allies and then spent a year putting down revolts across the empire, a campaign he had carved into the cliff at Behistun in three languages. He reorganised the realm into satrapies with fixed tribute, standardised coinage and law, built the Royal Road, and founded Persepolis.
entries.note: Behistun Inscription (DB), trilingual Old Persian/Elamite/Babylonian; Herodotus, Histories 3.61–88, 3.89–97 (tribute list).

entries.group: Xerxes and the Wars with Greece
entries.label: Xerxes I — the invasion of Greece
entries.hint: Xerxes suppressed revolts in Egypt and Babylon early in his reign, then led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC — forcing Thermopylae, burning Athens, and losing the fleet at Salamis before withdrawing. He completed Persepolis's Gate of All Nations and was assassinated in a palace conspiracy in 465 BC.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 7–9; Persepolis Gate of All Nations trilingual inscription (XPa).

entries.group: Xerxes and the Wars with Greece
entries.label: Artaxerxes I — the reordering of the succession
entries.hint: After the chiliarch Artabanus murdered Xerxes and moved to seize power, Xerxes's son Artaxerxes overthrew and killed him — also killing his own brother Darius, accused of the assassination, to secure the throne. His long reign saw the loss and reconquest of Egypt and, by tradition, a peace settlement with Athens.
entries.note: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius); Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–110 (the Egyptian revolt).

entries.label: Xerxes II — a forty-five day reign
entries.hint: The only son of Artaxerxes I born to a legitimate queen, Xerxes II held the throne for barely six weeks before being murdered in his sleep by his half-brother Sogdianus — the opening act of a succession crisis that would burn through three kings in a single year.
entries.note: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius, Bibliotheca 72).

entries.label: Sogdianus — a half-year on the throne
entries.hint: Sogdianus, son of a royal concubine, seized the throne by murdering his half-brother Xerxes II, then held it for barely half a year before another half-brother, Ochus — satrap of Hyrcania — marched on Susa and overthrew him in turn.
entries.note: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius, Bibliotheca 72).

entries.label: Darius II — the Hyrcanian satrap's throne
entries.hint: Ochus took the throne name Darius II after defeating Sogdianus. His queen Parysatis exercised major influence at court, and in the closing years of the Peloponnesian War his satraps funnelled Persian gold to Sparta's fleet, tipping the balance against Athens.
entries.note: Xenophon, Hellenica 1–2; Thucydides 8 (Persian-Spartan negotiations).

entries.label: Artaxerxes II — the longest reign
entries.hint: Artaxerxes survived his younger brother Cyrus the Younger's rebellion in the first years of his reign, held the throne for 46 years — the longest of any Achaemenid king — and dictated the terms of Greek interstate politics through the King's Peace of 387 BC after losing Egypt to a successful native revolt.
entries.note: Xenophon, Anabasis 1; Xenophon, Hellenica 5.1.31 (the King's Peace).

entries.label: Artaxerxes III — the reconquest of Egypt
entries.hint: Later Greek tradition accuses Artaxerxes III of executing rival relatives to secure his succession. He reconquered Egypt in 343 BC, ending the last native Egyptian dynasty, before being poisoned by his own chiliarch, the eunuch Bagoas.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 16.40–51 (the Egyptian campaign), 17.5 (the poisoning).

entries.label: Artaxerxes IV (Arses) — Bagoas's puppet
entries.hint: Bagoas installed the young Arses after poisoning Artaxerxes III and most other claimants to the throne. When Arses tried to act against him, Bagoas poisoned him too, after barely two years on the throne.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.5.

entries.label: Darius III — the fall of the empire
entries.hint: A collateral descendant of the royal line, Darius III was raised to the throne by Bagoas and promptly forced the kingmaker to drink his own poison. He lost the empire to Alexander's invasion across three pitched battles and was murdered by his own satrap Bessus in Bactria in 330 BC.
entries.note: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.5–6, 17.73 (the murder by Bessus); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.21.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Conquest, revolt, and the wars with Greece and Macedon

entries.label: Cyrus's Conquests — Media, Lydia and Babylon
entries.hint: In a single decade Cyrus overturned the political map of the Near East: he took Ecbatana from his grandfather Astyages (c.550 BC), captured Sardis from Croesus of Lydia (c.547 BC), and entered Babylon without a fight after Nabonidus's army collapsed at Opis (539 BC).
entries.note: Nabonidus Chronicle (BM 35382); Cyrus Cylinder (BM 90920); Herodotus, Histories 1.75–91, 1.153–214.

entries.label: Battle of Pelusium
entries.hint: Cambyses defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III's army at Pelusium on the eastern Delta frontier, opening the road to Memphis and ending Egypt's Twenty-Sixth (Saite) Dynasty as an independent power.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 3.10–13; Polyaenus, Strategemata 7.9 (the cats-as-shields tradition, treated with source-critical caution).

entries.label: The Ionian Revolt
entries.hint: The Greek cities of Ionia, led by Miletus's Aristagoras and briefly aided by Athens and Eretria, rose against Persian-appointed tyrants and satrapal rule. Darius crushed the revolt at the naval Battle of Lade (494 BC) and the sack of Miletus, but Athens's involvement gave him his pretext for invading Greece.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 5.28–6.32.

entries.label: The Greco-Persian Wars
entries.hint: Darius's punitive expedition was stopped at Marathon in 490 BC; Xerxes's far larger invasion a decade later forced the pass at Thermopylae and burned Athens, but lost its fleet at Salamis (480 BC) and its army at Plataea (479 BC), ending Persia's attempts to conquer the Greek mainland.

entries.label: Inaros's Revolt in Egypt
entries.hint: The Libyan prince Inaros led Egypt in revolt against Artaxerxes I with a large Athenian naval expeditionary force in support, defeating a Persian army at Papremis before the revolt was finally crushed and Inaros executed at Susa.
entries.note: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.104, 1.109–110; Ctesias, Persica (via Photius).

entries.label: Persian Subsidy of Sparta's Fleet
entries.hint: Darius II's satraps Tissaphernes and, later, the crown prince Cyrus the Younger financed the Spartan war effort against Athens in exchange for a free hand over the Greek cities of Asia Minor — Persian gold that proved decisive in Athens's final naval defeat.
entries.note: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 8.5–6, 8.18 (the treaties with Sparta); Xenophon, Hellenica 1–2.

entries.group: The March of the Ten Thousand
entries.label: Battle of Cunaxa and the March of the Ten Thousand
entries.hint: Cyrus the Younger marched a Persian and Greek mercenary army against his brother Artaxerxes II, dying in the moment of near-victory at Cunaxa. The stranded Greek mercenaries' fighting retreat north to the Black Sea, chronicled by Xenophon, exposed the empire's western vulnerability a generation before Alexander.
entries.note: Xenophon, Anabasis, books 1–4.

entries.label: Alexander's Conquest of the Empire
entries.hint: Alexander defeated Darius III in three pitched battles — the Granicus (334 BC), Issus (333 BC), and the decisive Gaugamela (331 BC) — before occupying Babylon, Susa and Persepolis and pursuing the fleeing king into Bactria, where Darius was murdered by his own satrap Bessus.
entries.note: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 1–3; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The satrapy system, imperial law, and the fiscal machinery of empire

entries.label: The Satrapy System
entries.hint: Darius I divided the empire into roughly twenty provinces (satrapies), each under a satrap balanced by an independent military commander and royal inspectors — the 'King's Eyes and Ears' — who reported directly to the throne, a structural check against provincial autonomy.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.6.16 (the King's Eyes).

entries.label: The Fixed Tribute Assessment
entries.hint: Herodotus preserves what appears to be an administrative document: a satrapy-by-satrap list of annual tribute owed in silver talents, from Ionia and Babylon's wealth down to Ethiopia's gold and India's gold dust — the earliest surviving imperial tax schedule from the ancient Near East.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97.

entries.label: The Daric — Imperial Gold Coinage
entries.hint: Darius I reserved the minting of gold coin (the daric, named for him) as a royal monopoly, while satraps and cities could strike silver — a two-tier currency system that made gold coinage itself a symbol of Achaemenid sovereignty across the empire's Mediterranean-facing provinces.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 4.166; surviving daric specimens, British Museum and Cabinet des Médailles.

entries.label: The Law of the Medes and Persians
entries.hint: Later sources describe an Achaemenid legal principle that a king's sealed decree, once issued, could not be revoked even by the king himself — a constitutional constraint on royal power that appears in both the Book of Esther and the Book of Daniel as a narrative device reflecting a real administrative reputation.
entries.note: Book of Esther 1:19, 8:8; Book of Daniel 6:8–15; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.30.

entries.label: Cyrus's Edict for Jerusalem
entries.hint: The Book of Ezra records a decree of Cyrus authorising the Judean exiles in Babylon to return home and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, funded in part from the royal treasury — consistent with the general policy of restoring local cults and returning displaced peoples that the Cyrus Cylinder claims for Babylon itself.
entries.note: Ezra 1:1–4, 6:3–5; Cyrus Cylinder (BM 90920) for the parallel general policy.

entries.label: Darius and the Codification of Egyptian Law
entries.hint: The Demotic Chronicle records that Darius I ordered Egyptian priests and officials to compile the country's laws 'down to year 44 of Amasis' into a single code — an act of governance through the deliberate patronage and continuity of a subject people's own legal tradition, not its replacement.
entries.note: Demotic Chronicle (Papyrus Bibliothèque Nationale 215), verso; Hibis Temple dedication, Kharga Oasis.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Ahura Mazda, the Magi, and the religions of a multi-ethnic empire

entries.label: Ahura Mazda in Royal Ideology
entries.hint: Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam declares Ahura Mazda the greatest of gods who made Darius king — but the same text also acknowledges 'the other gods who are', a formula that cautions against reading full Zoroastrian orthodoxy, as later codified under the Sasanians, back into Achaemenid royal religion.
entries.note: Naqsh-e Rustam inscription of Darius I (DNa).

entries.label: The Magi as Ritual Specialists
entries.hint: Herodotus names the Magi as one of the Median tribes and describes their distinctive funerary practice — exposing the dead to birds and dogs before burial — alongside their role interpreting royal dreams and officiating at sacrifice, evidence for a specialised priesthood distinct from the general population's practice.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 1.101, 1.140.

entries.label: The Return from Exile and the Second Temple
entries.hint: Following Cyrus's decree, groups of Judean exiles returned to Jerusalem under Sheshbazzar and later Zerubbabel; the rebuilt Temple was completed and dedicated in the sixth year of Darius I, 516 BC, after delays the Book of Ezra attributes to local opposition and a change of Persian administration.
entries.note: Ezra 1–6; Book of Haggai (dated to Darius's second year, 520 BC).

entries.label: Nehemiah's Mission and the Walls of Jerusalem
entries.hint: Nehemiah, a cupbearer at Artaxerxes I's court, obtained royal authorisation and letters of safe passage to rebuild Jerusalem's walls — an unusually detailed first-person Judean account of how a subject community secured and used imperial favour.
entries.note: Book of Nehemiah 1–6.

entries.group: Babylonian & Egyptian Cults under Persian Rule
entries.label: The Cyrus Cylinder and the Restoration of Marduk
entries.hint: Composed by or for Babylon's own priesthood, the Cyrus Cylinder casts Cyrus as the choice of the god Marduk, sent to end Nabonidus's neglect of the cult and restore proper temple worship — royal legitimation expressed entirely in the conquered city's own religious idiom.
entries.note: Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum ME 90920).

entries.group: Babylonian & Egyptian Cults under Persian Rule
entries.label: The Apis Bulls of Memphis
entries.hint: Herodotus claims Cambyses stabbed the sacred Apis bull in a fit of impiety, but a stela from the Serapeum at Saqqara records an Apis burial performed and inscribed in Cambyses's own name in 524 BC — archaeological evidence that directly contradicts the hostile Greek literary tradition about Persian rule in Egypt.
entries.note: Serapeum Apis stela of Year 6 of Cambyses (Louvre); Herodotus, Histories 3.27–29, for the tradition it contradicts.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Persepolis, Pasargadae, and the art of universal kingship

entries.label: Persepolis — the Apadana and the Gate of All Nations
entries.hint: Founded by Darius I as a ceremonial capital, Persepolis's terraced complex — the great audience hall (Apadana), the monumental Gate of All Nations, and the Hundred-Column Hall completed under Xerxes and Artaxerxes I — was built to stage the New Year's (Nowruz) reception of tribute from across the empire.
entries.note: Persepolis Apadana foundation tablets (DPh, DPf); excavation reports, Oriental Institute of Chicago (Erich Schmidt, 1930s).

entries.label: The Tomb of Cyrus at Pasargadae
entries.hint: Cyrus's tomb — a gabled stone chamber raised on a stepped plinth, standing apart from the palace terraces — combines Elamite platform-building with Anatolian and Mesopotamian elements, an early statement of the composite visual language the dynasty would use throughout its architecture.
entries.note: Pasargadae excavations, David Stronach (1961–63); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 6.29 (Alexander's visit and restoration of the tomb).

entries.label: The Apadana Reliefs — Twenty-Three Nations
entries.hint: The staircases of the Apadana carry processional reliefs of delegations from twenty-three subject peoples — Medes, Elamites, Babylonians, Egyptians, Indians, Scythians and others — each in distinct dress, bringing characteristic gifts, a visual encyclopaedia of imperial diversity staged as willing tribute.
entries.note: Persepolis Apadana staircase reliefs, in situ; Walser, Die Völkerschaften auf den Reliefs von Persepolis (1966).

entries.label: The Behistun Relief
entries.hint: Carved above the trilingual inscription, the relief shows Darius standing with his foot on the prostrate Gaumata while nine bound rebel kings await judgement before him — royal ideology rendered as image for an audience that could not read the cuneiform text beneath it.
entries.note: Behistun relief and inscription (DB), in situ, Kermanshah Province, Iran.

entries.label: The Oxus Treasure
entries.loc: Found: Oxus riverbank (Takht-i Kuwad, Tajikistan) · Now: British Museum, London
entries.hint: A hoard of some 180 gold and silver objects — armlets terminating in griffin heads, votive plaques, a model chariot — recovered from the Oxus riverbank, the richest surviving assemblage of Achaemenid court metalwork from the empire's northeastern satrapies.
entries.note: British Museum, Oxus Treasure collection (ANE 123901 and related accessions); O.M. Dalton, The Treasure of the Oxus (1905).

entries.label: Court Musicians in the Persepolis Fortification Archive
entries.hint: Among the tens of thousands of administrative tablets recording rations issued to workers and travellers at Persepolis, a number list payments to named singers and musicians attached to the royal court — direct bureaucratic evidence for professional court music-making, independent of any later literary description.
entries.note: Persepolis Fortification Archive (PF-NN texts); Wouter Henkelman, The Other Gods Who Are (2008), on court personnel categories.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Royal ideology, Greek historiography, and geographic knowledge

entries.label: Truth and the Lie — Behistun's Ideology of Kingship
entries.hint: Darius's inscription frames his year of civil war as a cosmic struggle between arta (truth/order) and drauga (the Lie) — every rebel is a 'Lie-follower' and Darius the restorer of truth under Ahura Mazda's favour, a legitimating formula repeated in later royal inscriptions across the dynasty.
entries.note: Behistun Inscription (DB) §§4, 54–58, 63–69.

entries.label: Herodotus's Histories
entries.hint: Herodotus of Halicarnassus, himself a subject of the Persian empire by birth, composed the first extended narrative history of the Greek world's conflict with Persia — the dominant external source for Achaemenid political history, valuable and frequently unreliable in the same passages, and read against Persian inscriptions wherever they survive.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories, esp. books 1, 3, 7–9.

entries.label: Scylax's Voyage down the Indus
entries.hint: Darius I commissioned the Carian navigator Scylax of Caryanda to sail down the Indus and around the Arabian Peninsula to Egypt, mapping a sea route that fed directly into the annexation of the Indus valley as a satrapy and the completion of a Nile–Red Sea canal.
entries.note: Herodotus, Histories 4.44.

entries.label: The Arshama Letters
entries.loc: Provenance: Egypt (probably Elephantine region) · Now: Bodleian Library, Oxford
entries.hint: A cache of Aramaic letters from Arshama, the absentee Achaemenid satrap of Egypt, to his estate managers survives on leather — day-to-day instructions on runaway slaves, estate income and staff, giving an unusually intimate view of how a satrap actually governed at a distance.
entries.note: Bodleian Library Aramaic Documents of Arshama; Tuplin & Ma (eds.), Aramaic Documents from Achaemenid Egypt (Oxford, 2020).
